findings.question: q-statistics-and-probability-measures-of-variability-0004
findings.problem: The keyed choice is the only short fragment. All three distractors are full sentences beginning with “The range.” This makes the answer stand out by its form and lets a student use the wording pattern instead of knowing how range is defined.
findings.fix: Write all four choices as parallel definitions of similar length.

findings.question: q-statistics-and-probability-measures-of-variability-0005
findings.quote: The square root of population variance.
findings.problem: The keyed choice is a short definition fragment, while every distractor is a much longer sentence beginning with “It is.” A student can identify the unusually phrased choice without understanding standard deviation.
findings.fix: Use parallel definition fragments of comparable length for all four choices.

findings.question: q-statistics-and-probability-measures-of-variability-0012
findings.quote: Route A has more consistent times.
findings.problem: The keyed choice is a short, direct statement, while each distractor is roughly three times as long. This repeats the conspicuous short-answer pattern in questions 0004 and 0005 and offers a cue independent of comparing standard deviations.
findings.fix: Make the route comparisons parallel and similar in length.

findings.question: q-statistics-and-probability-measures-of-variability-0015
findings.quote: The sample mean is fitted to the sample itself, which makes deviations smaller on average than deviations from the unknown population mean. Dividing their squared sum by $n$ would underestimate population variance on average. Dividing by $n-1$ corrects this bias under the stated random-sample assumptions.
findings.problem: “Fitted,” “bias,” and “under the stated random-sample assumptions” leave the reasoning in technical exam language. In particular, “bias” is never explained, so a Grade 5 reader is not told plainly what the correction fixes.
findings.fix: Explain that the sample average comes from those same values, making the calculated spread tend to be too small; dividing by one less raises the estimate and corrects that tendency over many samples.
